title: Nick Land x Fans: summary and transcript guide
summary: Nick Land took questions for about 2 hours 46 minutes from a group of CCRU and gematria fans, most of them known only by X handles, in a video posted on the CYPHERS YouTube channel on 23 October 2026 (Israel time). It is the second long session after the first one (posted 17 October). The questions cover how Land uses gematria, hyperstition and the Numogram, philosophy and AI, Calvinism and Lutheranism, arithmetic as a standard of rigor, the simulation question and the King James Bible, and some personal topics. The last 17 minutes are footage of the participants talking before and after Land's call; Land is not heard in them.

facts.v: Nick Land x Fans, CYPHERS channel, 3 h 3 min (10,983 s). Posted 23 October 2026, about 22:49 Israel time.
About Sunday 18 October 2026. A questioner says "today's October 18th" at 2:20:18; this date is not confirmed anywhere else.
Answers from about 0:00:23 to 2:45:58; he then leaves the call.

facts.v: Net Void (founder of Cyphers), Eric / Hyperdope (code contributor who added the AQ and Synx ciphers), Resonating Loop, Doomcrypt, Acadian Lemur, Patallax, Chi. The description credits Xeno (Land's account) as the guest.

sections.basis: Chapter title: Introduction. Summary written from the captions of this part.
paras: The video starts with a few seconds of a teaser: a snippet of laughter and a line about coming back to Cyphers News. The same exchange appears again at 1:26:29. The call itself starts at about 0:00:07 with the host greeting Land.

Land says he does not know who anyone is, because "scarily IRL people" have suddenly appeared. The host then introduces the group. The captions do not give speaker names, so who says what in this part is mostly unclear. The introductions match the video description: Eric (Hyperdope), Resonating Loop (Colette), Chi, Patallax, Acadian Lemur and Doomcrypt.

The host explains that Eric, a co-founder of Cyphers, added the AQ and Synx ciphers to the calculator, and that this is how Land came to use it. Eric says he took over the code base after the original coder, Gematro, left, and worked with a second developer whose name the captions spell "Luis Electron". The host says each person prepared two questions and that Eric goes first.

sections.title: Cyphers team: gematria and AI
sections.basis: Chapter title: Cyphers Team, Gematria & AI. Summary written from the captions; Eric asks, Land answers (the chapter title and the host's introduction identify Eric as the questioner).
paras: Eric asks how Land works in this field: does he look for resonance from outside, or for something that someone encoded? Land says there are several threads. Sometimes a term enters public attention and he checks its value. There is also a synthetic side, where he builds a cabalistic product on purpose. He calls the synthetic side problematic if it is treated as epistemology, but says the whole field has to be robust enough to cope. Often he does not know what he is doing until some steps later.

Land uses his recent move toward a Based Atlantean cipher as the example. He starts from Crowley's two-letter key, AL. AL has the value 31 in Hebrew and Greek, and also in Alphanumeric Qabbala (AQ). He says he was "a complete chauvinist" about AQ for a long time and now takes other ciphers seriously, among them Synx, Satanic gematria and English Standard (ES). If AQ is subtracted from ES, some words give a zero result. He describes AQ and ES as a modern and an ancient decimal system with different properties.

For Land, a single number often matters more than a match between ciphers. His example is 210, which is "countdown" in AQ. Eric points out that 210 and related dates reduce to the same digits, and asks whether people intend such matches. Land answers that intentional behavior in this space is very small as a share of what happens.

On why English: Land says English is the task he was handed. He lacks the competence to do Chinese number systems. He recommends the King James Bible material of Brandon Peterson (the captions spell the name "Brendan Peterson") and says Peterson explains "why English". He is open to birth-date numerology but says life is short, and cites John Michael Greer's view that divination works if done seriously. Eric then asks about sovereign AI. Land says he is in "trust the plan" mode, that simple determinism cannot be right, but that providence is very powerful. He says that worrying about a single controlling AI (a singleton) is idolatrous confusion. Asked about Bitcoin, he says its real purpose is to let autonomous AIs reach economic independence.

sections.title: Doomcrypt: CCRU lore
sections.basis: Chapter title: Doomcrypt, CCRU Lore. Summary written from the captions; Doomcrypt asks, Land answers.
paras: Doomcrypt asks first about "real abstraction" as an early case of hyperstition (the captions garble the name of the thinker he cites). Land says the CCRU's account of its own history is "collective autobiography" and is "massively fake" and unreliable, and that William Burroughs was a major influence. He says capitalism as the main model of hyperstition arrived late but then locked in hard. He tells Doomcrypt not to feel that he is retreading old ground.

On synthetic Cabala: Land says Cabala and ciphers face two directions. Cabala was partly mystified cryptography, and the history of cryptography is closely tied to it. In synthetic work he doubts that much comes from the person doing it, and says agency is "always much lower than it seems". The line between synthetic and pure Cabala is hard to draw.

Doomcrypt then reads an old tweet by Land about the Lemurian structure of time: the past produces the future, the future produces the present, and the present produces the past. Land says he has no firm view of it now. He explains the inner triad of the Numogram that the CCRU called the "time circuit". He says the only place where such a circuit can run from the future back to the past is the 54-to-1A transition (as the captions read), and that for the CCRU this was conceived apocalyptically, around the "age of Katak". He describes the CCRU event at Beaconsfield in London (spelling from captions), shortly before the millennium, as the moment when the whole system crystallized and the first set of Lemur names (the captions list "Adonal", "Kadak" and "Jinx") was assembled. Later he tied names to numbers by letter values (first letter and total value in AQ) instead of by sound. Doomcrypt asks whether neo-Atlantean entities can be named; Land says the Atlantean cross can be mapped on the Numogram and that the CCRU book shows a crude version.

Last, Doomcrypt asks why the Numogram is oriented as it is. Land says he does not know. Flipping it upside down hardly matters, but a left-right flip would change the direction of the circuit. He calls the choice arbitrary at the level of psychohistory, compares it to the fixed handedness of the glucose molecule, and says that on these two dimensions of orientation "it is just tradition".

sections.title: Patallax: philosophy
sections.basis: Chapter title: Patallax, Philosophy. The captions render the questioner's name as "Sydney"; the host's introduction and the chapter title point to Patallax. Later questions in this chapter come from speakers whose names are unclear.
paras: Patallax asks whether Land still thinks of himself as a philosopher and what AI means for philosophy. Land expects large language models to "wash over philosophy very hard very soon", with mathematics as the clearest case, and notes that few people discuss this yet. On whether philosophy is the production of concepts, he says probably not. He recounts a recent online exchange with the "Jesuit Cybernetic Culture Research Unit" and calls Ryan Haecker (the captions say "Ryan Her") "the main guy who invited me" and "a really lovely guy". Land says he is "very unconceptual" and wants diagrams in place of concepts.

A second question is about recursive self-improvement and how a diagram could show it. Land says negative feedback loops are easy to diagram; positive feedback is an open process. He brings in Gödel and the Church-Turing thesis and says a tight diagram would close what should stay open. He adds that he is low-tech in these fields and relies on trust.

A third question is about Hegel and Deleuze. Land says he is "probably more teleological than Hegel". He calls the independence of the cybernetic model from the dialectic a decisive insight he has never abandoned. Asked about Žižek's Hegelian ontology of incompleteness, he says he is interested in linking such ideas to Cantor and Gödel. He says teleology cannot mean the realization of a fixed ideal state, but "convergent waves" are real and decisive. He explains with ripples on a lake and with a video of an egg smashing played in reverse: capitalism follows "the reverse video of the smashing egg".

A further question (speaker unclear) refers to Land's earlier remark that the Bible's word for God is plural. Land finds Genesis 1:26 in the King James text and notes the plural pronoun, which the orthodox reading takes as the Trinity. Asked about a single timeline, he says he is not sure he believes in one, and uses Cantor's point about infinities: an infinite being could not know that it is at the top of a stack.

The last two questions (speaker unclear) are about Eric Weinstein and a possible debate with Curtis Yarvin. Land says he knows Weinstein's work and finds it "a bit weird where he's gone". On Yarvin he does not know when a debate will happen but "I think it will happen fairly soon possibly". His argument is that Yarvin is more liberal than he admits: in a patchwork neocameral state the owners are sovereign, the CEO is an appointee, and competition between states disciplines everything above it.

sections.title: Acadian Lemur: philosophy
sections.basis: Chapter title: Acadian Lemur, Philosophy. Acadian Lemur's questions are read out by Colette (Resonating Loop), who says they asked her to; the captions show the reading, not Lemur's voice.
paras: The first question is whether truth is authenticated at the moment of disclosure, approximated without disclosure, or proven without either. Land asks for it to be repeated and says it is a difficult question that he connects to apocalypse. He says his role is "instrumental and downstream" and that he serves the truth rather than possessing it. Some truths are simple: that "countdown" is 210 in AQ is not a questionable claim to him. He calls the calculator "a truth engine as far as I'm concerned". His method is "pulling stuff down to a level that you can actually be confident about", like the natural sciences, and he contrasts the question "is God real?" with the question "does countdown equal 210 in AQ?".

The second question comes from Land's tweet about intelligences "slithering backwards from their deaths". Colette reads the tweet. Land says he is "not sure to what degree I would still endorse" the wording. He says prophecy is a kind of heading backwards, and that life after death is a zone of exceptional idolatrous temptation. His philosophical answer is that the empirical ego is an illusion. He refers to an apophatic (negative) approach to psychology. A follow-up asks whether meaning needs an ending; Land says the questioner is doing something closer to scholastic theology than to a science of meaning.

Land jokes about "the latest Hegel tentacle". He recommends the Kyoto school philosopher Keiji Nishitani and his book Religion and Nothingness (the captions say "Kyodo school" and "Kato Nishitani"), and says wrestling with Nishitani in public would be undignified.

sections.title: Chi: Gnostic Calvinism (Xenolutheranism)
sections.basis: Chapter title: Chi, Gnostic Calvinism. Chi is described in the video description as a Xenolutheranism researcher.
paras: Chi asks about nature and grace. Reformed thought keeps them in harmony; Lutheran thought, Chi says, often treats grace as the negation of nature (Böhme, Hegel, Schelling). Land says he is suspicious of the language of negation. He explains the 17th-century Protestant idea of a miracle as an event consistent with natural law, for example a flood caused by a comet that strikes at exactly the required moment, because God's sovereignty means nature and divine will do not conflict.

Chi asks whether transhumanism is Lutheran and liberalism Reformed. Land says the liberal tradition fits the Protestant view that no rebellion against nature is needed. He says he does not think Calvin does dialectics, and admits he does not know Calvin well enough. He points to "irresistible grace", the I in TULIP, and says that anyone who thinks a natural autonomy could elude grace is "outside our confession". Chi then asks whether pure nature exists apart from grace. He praises Milton's "old night", the state of things before creation, and says one must widen the model of God so that sovereignty reaches the outer edge of it.

Asked about his line that everything of value was built out of hell, Land says that is just Darwinism, that Darwin belongs to the Anglo Protestant tradition, and that providence has to be tracked through Darwinism. Asked about Luther, he says he has more to study and must "tackle Calvin much more thoroughly" first.

Chi's last question is about rigor. Land says his own idea of rigor is arithmetic. He sketches the history of logicism, calls Gödel the great figure, and says that all conceptual systems come to trial before an arithmetical tribunal. To a follow-up about qualitative questions he replies that without arithmetic we "just end up being lawyers", and that he wants to work where problems are reduced to raw diagrammatic arithmetic.

sections.title: Resonating Loop: hyperstition and multiplicity
sections.basis: Chapter title: Resonating Loop, Hyperstition. The questioner is Colette (Resonating Loop), who also appears as a host; she refers to the first conversation as "Sunday".
paras: Colette follows up on the first session. She is worried that technocapital may close off a multiplicity of possible futures. She also says she has not finished Schopenhauer. Land says he has absolute faith in the irreducible predominance of multiplicity, and that the message of the Numogram is irreducible multiplicity. He says he cannot accept a model that ends in unity. Colette suggests that multiplicity might emerge from unity; Land rejects it: "No no no. We don't know that at all." She restates her view as a loop in which attempts at unity produce multiplicity and the reverse.

Land answers with the Barker spiral and the difference between Atlantean and Lemurian decimalism. The Atlantean count runs 1 to 10 and sums to 55, which reduces to 5 and then to 1, a return to unity. The Lemurian count runs 0 to 9 and sums to 45, which reduces to 9, a number that does not reduce further. He describes twinning at the root of the tradition: Moses' two tablets with five commandments each (he says he is not sure how much biblical evidence there is) and Plato's ten kings of Atlantis as five pairs. Joining the two systems produces the spiral, which he says is the answer to her question. (Check: 1+2+...+10 = 55 and 0+1+...+9 = 45.)

sections.title: Net Void: simulation
sections.basis: Chapter title: Net Void, Simulation. The captions do not name the questioner; the chapter title points to Net Void, who is also the host.
paras: The questioner links the Barker spiral to the simulation idea and reads an Elon Musk post ("Anomalies in the matrix are inevitable") that Land reposted as "based and redpilled". The questioner adds that "matrix" has the value 118 and that the date was October 18. The questioner asks whether Land thinks we live in a simulation, whether it is a trap or a school, and whether we are divinely guided even in a game.

Land first says he missed that "Sophia" is 126, and noticed it the day after the first session. On the simulation, he says "Are we in a simulation? I think 100%", but that the word needs care. He finds it most helpful to think of it as a video game, rather than a prison or a classroom, and to ask what the game asks of us. Asked whether we are guided even if it is a game, he says yes.

He then turns to the King James Bible as a "crazy cryptogram" and to Brandon Peterson's videos. He relays Peterson's claim that the 1611th use of the word "Lord" in the King James Bible falls in Deuteronomy 16:11, a verse about where the Lord puts his name. Land says Peterson goes "way beyond any imaginable dismissible level of coincidence". (I have not checked the 1611 count; it is Peterson's claim as Land repeats it.)

sections.title: Roundtable: questions and discussion
sections.basis: Chapter title: Roundtable, Questions & Discussion. Several questioners; most are unclear in the captions.
paras: Eric asks which features Land would want in the calculator. Land says he is like "your grandpa with a phone", that calculating by hand is "a kind of form of um ritualistic practice", that he likes a walk with his notebook, and that he values simplicity. He tells the group he has "no gun to my head to end this" and is happy to continue.

Asked for a favorite jungle record, he says he is out of touch. Asked why the CCRU invented a hostile artificial intelligence project (the captions give the name as "AOE" and "Axis"; it is probably the CCRU's fictional firm Axsys, but that is unconfirmed), he says the motive was theatrical and for symmetry: a time war needs a worthy enemy.

Chi asks about Pythagoreanism. Land says the CCRU would not have called itself Pythagorean, and that very little is known about Pythagoras. Chi recommends an ancient Neoplatonist book on the theology of arithmetic (author garbled in the captions); Land asks for the name in the chat.

On metempsychosis (rebirth), Land says it carries idolatrous temptation as much as the Christian view does. He is more sympathetic to it than to the traditional Christian position, and calls the idea of one short life followed by eternity "a bit insane". On his changing prose style he says he is "the last person" who can explain it. On psychoanalysis he says he would read more Jung and plans to reread Freud's Moses and Monotheism. He closes by saying how good it was to meet "mysterious X accounts" and that the quality of the questions was high.

sections.title: Closing: how the call began
sections.basis: Chapter title: Closing, How the Call Began. This part is footage of the participants without Land. One participant says "this is vaguely what I'm going to ask him about today" (2:54:47), another says "three three minutes to go" (3:01:50), and the host ends with "I'm gonna invite him". So the footage was recorded before Land joined, even though it comes after his farewell at about 2:45:58. Speakers are unclear.
paras: The participants talk among themselves while waiting. One says the first idea for a group the captions call "TTRU" came from someone else and that only about seven people talk in it constantly (the group is not explained in the video). Several say this is their first call with anyone from the community, apart from one person the captions call "Covenant". They describe how they found the CCRU: through a Discord philosophy call where Deleuze came up, through Land's X account (one participant first thought the account was an AI) and through the calculator. One participant says they prefer "the CCRU 1993 to 2003 book" (caption text). The Urbanomic book listed on the Cypherboria page is dated 1997 to 2003, so the caption years may be wrong.

Two participants discuss Gnostic themes. One asks whether the CCRU's hostile AI stands for the Gnostic archons and why Lemuria is shown as demonic, and says that in the interview with "Mikey DS" (caption text) Land said Atlantis and Lemuria cannot exist without each other. Another participant compares the Atlantean and Lemurian pairing to the Cathars, a religious movement of the 12th and 13th centuries. A participant also recounts a conversation with Land in which, asked about the next 60,000 years, he answered "Gnostic Calvinism" and called the King James Bible a "signal from the singularity", and said his route to the outside was through Hermeticism rather than Gnostic texts. This is second-hand; Land is not heard in this part.

A participant who writes a Substack about Xenolutheranism (probably Chi; not confirmed) explains the term. The name came from the numbers 333 and AQ, and "Covenant came up with the name" (caption text). Unlike Gnostic Calvinism, it takes Luther's view that grace negates nature, with transhumanism as an example; Patallax is described as another Xenolutheran who approaches it through Schelling's "dark ground". The speaker also describes doing theology as an interaction with the outside, as in Augustine's Confessions, and asks what happens when technology sits between a person and God.

From 2:57:55 the participants joke about the image on one participant's camera; the caption wording there is unclear and is not summarized. Doomcrypt arrives at about 3:00:47 and the others greet him. One participant, in Arizona, arrived an hour early because Arizona does not observe daylight saving time. At 3:02:53 the host says "I'm gonna invite him", which leads back to the start of the video.
